issues.legal_issue: A trespasser in settled possession may exercise the criminal-law right of private defence of property against an attempt by the true owner to dispossess them by force.
material_facts: The appellants took actual possession of the land about a month before the occurrence, and the complainant knew that they had been dispossessed.
The appellants had grown a wheat crop on the land.
The complainant party went to the land armed and attempted to retake possession and destroy the crop.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were in settled possession and could defend their possession against the complainant party, even though they were trespassers.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 96 to 105 of the Indian Penal Code, as applied in Munshi Ram and Others v. Delhi Administration, a trespasser whose possession is settled may defend it against the true owner. Settled possession is not determined by a rigid time period: it requires actual physical possession over a sufficiently long period, possession known to the owner or not concealed and held with an intention to possess, completed and final dispossession acquiesced in by the owner, and, for cultivable land, may be shown by the trespasser having grown a crop. The Court explained Munshi Ram and relied on Horam v. Rex, Sangappa v. State, In re Mooka Nadar, Hazara Singh v. State, Bhartu v. State and Phula Singh v. Emperor.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_private_defence_claim and actual_physical_possession_over_sufficient_period and possession_known_to_owner_or_not_concealed and completed_dispossession_acquiesced_in_by_owner and crop_grown_on_cultivable_land

predicates.criminal_case_with_private_defence_claim: The proceeding is a criminal case in which an accused claims a right to defend possession of property.
predicates.actual_physical_possession_over_sufficie: The accused had actual physical possession of the property for a period sufficient, in the circumstances, to distinguish it from a stray or casual act of possession.
predicates.possession_known_to_owner_or_not_conceal: The owner knew, expressly or impliedly, of the accused's possession, or the accused did not try to conceal it and possessed the property with an intention to possess it.
predicates.completed_dispossession_acquiesced_in_by: The accused had completed the dispossession of the owner, and the owner acquiesced in that dispossession before attempting to retake the property.
predicates.crop_grown_on_cultivable_land: The accused had grown a crop on the cultivable land after taking possession.

issues.definition: When an accused in a criminal case has sufficiently long, known or open possession, has completed the dispossession with the owner's acquiescence, and has grown a crop on cultivable land, the accused may defend that possession against forcible dispossession.

issues.legal_issue: A person defending settled possession may use force, including force causing death, where an immediate invasion and a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt justify it, and the response is assessed in the circumstances rather than by exact measurement of each blow.
material_facts: The appellants were in possession of the land and had grown wheat there.
The complainant party went to the land armed with weapons and attempted to destroy the crop and retake possession by force.
Two appellants' associates suffered gunshot injuries, which the prosecution did not explain.
The prosecution's account did not disclose the material origin of the occurrence.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were entitled to defend their property and persons, and the Court could not find that they had exceeded that right, including in causing the deaths.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 99 to 102 of the Indian Penal Code govern the limitations and operation of private defence. A person facing an immediate attack need not flee to the authorities; where there is an invasion or aggression by a person without a right to possession, there may be no opportunity to seek their aid. Under Jai Dev v. State of Punjab and Amjad Khan v. State, reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt is enough to activate the right, and the response is not judged by weighing blows in golden scales. The right may extend to causing death where that apprehension exists. The Court also followed State of Gujarat v. Sai Fatima on the assessment of injuries to accused persons and the circumstances of an occurrence.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_private_defence_claim and settled_possession_attacked_by_forcible_invasion and aggressor_armed_or_using_serious_violence and reasonable_apprehension_of_death_or_grievous_hurt and response_assessed_in_immediate_circumstances

predicates.criminal_case_with_private_defence_claim: The proceeding is a criminal case in which an accused claims a right of private defence of person or property.
predicates.settled_possession_attacked_by_forcible_: The accused was in settled possession of property when another person attempted to invade that possession or retake the property by force.
predicates.aggressor_armed_or_using_serious_violenc: The person making the invasion was armed or used violence serious enough to create an immediate danger.
predicates.reasonable_apprehension_of_death_or_grie: The circumstances gave the accused a reasonable apprehension that death or grievous hurt might be caused to the accused or another person.
predicates.response_assessed_in_immediate_circumsta: The accused responded during the attack, in circumstances requiring a prompt reaction rather than allowing time for measured reflection.

issues.definition: When a person in settled possession faces a forcible, serious attack that reasonably creates fear of death or grievous hurt, their defensive response is assessed in the immediate circumstances and may be found not to exceed the right of private defence.

issues.legal_issue: A prosecution fails to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt where the accused's injuries are left unexplained and the prosecution suppresses material evidence about how the occurrence began, in circumstances supporting private defence or casting doubt on the prosecution account.
material_facts: Two persons on the appellants' side had injuries, including gunshot injuries, and the prosecution gave no explanation for them.
The prosecution deliberately suppressed a material part of the origin of the occurrence.
The evidence supported the appellants' account that the complainant party had come armed to retake the land and destroy the crop.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were protected by private defence, and in any event the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt; the convictions and sentences were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under State of Gujarat v. Sai Fatima, unexplained injuries on an accused may, depending on the facts, support a finding that the accused acted in self-defence, make the prosecution version doubtful so that the charge is not proved beyond reasonable doubt, or have no effect on the prosecution case. Where the prosecution suppresses the material origin of the occurrence, the resulting uncertainty may also prevent the prosecution from proving its case beyond reasonable doubt.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution_for_violent_offence and accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries and prosecution_suppressed_material_origin and evidence_supports_private_defence_or_doubt

predicates.criminal_prosecution_for_violent_offence: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution alleging that the accused committed a violent offence.
predicates.accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries: One or more accused persons sustained injuries during the occurrence, and the prosecution did not explain them.
predicates.prosecution_suppressed_material_origin: The prosecution withheld or suppressed material evidence about how the occurrence began.
predicates.evidence_supports_private_defence_or_dou: The evidence supports a claim of private defence or otherwise leaves reasonable doubt about the prosecution account.

issues.definition: In a violent-offence prosecution, unexplained injuries to the accused and suppression of how the occurrence began, together with evidence supporting private defence or doubt, mean that the prosecution case is not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
